Renal & body fluids.question: ১) Which is in the anterior relation of right kidney?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The anterior relations of the right kidney include the second part of the duodenum, liver, right colic flexure, and jejunal/ileal loops. Among the given options, the 2nd part of the duodenum is the classic and most important anterior relation.

The splenic flexure and descending colon are related to the left kidney, while the jejunum is more characteristically related to the left kidney.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Kidney Important anterior relations
Right 2nd part of duodenum, liver, right colic flexure, jejunal/ileal loops
Left Stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum, descending colon

Exam Pearl:
Right kidney → 2nd part of duodenum; Left kidney → stomach, spleen, pancreas, descending colon.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২) Which is the outermost covering of kidney?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The kidney is surrounded by several coverings arranged from inside → outside:

Fibrous capsule → Perirenal fat → Renal fascia → Pararenal fat

Therefore, the outermost covering is pararenal (paranephric) fat.

  • Fibrous capsule → directly covers the kidney.

  • Perirenal fat → surrounds the fibrous capsule.

  • Renal fascia (Gerota’s fascia) → encloses the kidney and perirenal fat.

  • Pararenal fat → lies outside the renal fascia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:
Kidney coverings:
Fibrous capsule → Perirenal fat → Renal fascia → Pararenal fat

Exam Pearl:
Outermost = Pararenal fat.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৩) Which is the initial dilated portion of renal cortex?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The renal corpuscle is the initial dilated portion of the nephron and is located in the renal cortex. It consists of the glomerulus surrounded by Bowman’s capsule. It is the site where blood filtration begins.

The nephron sequence is:

Renal corpuscle → PCT → Loop of Henle → DCT → collecting duct

  • PCT → follows the renal corpuscle.

  • DCT → follows the loop of Henle.

  • Renal pyramid → part of the renal medulla, not cortex.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renal corpuscle = Glomerulus + Bowman’s capsule

  • Location → renal cortex

  • Function → ultrafiltration of blood

  • First part of nephron → renal corpuscle

Exam Pearl:
Initial dilated portion of the nephron in the renal cortex = renal corpuscle.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৪) Which results from nonunion of the secretory and collecting parts of kidney?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Rosette kidney results from failure of fusion between the secretory portions (nephrons) and the collecting portions (collecting ducts) of the developing kidney. Normally, the ureteric bud forms the collecting system and interacts with the metanephric blastema, whose cells form the nephrons. Their connection is essential for a functional nephron–collecting duct system. Failure of this union can produce a rosette appearance of the renal tissue.

  • Horseshoe kidney → fusion of lower poles of kidneys.

  • Polycystic kidney → abnormal cyst formation.

  • Lobulated kidney → persistence of fetal lobulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Nonunion of secretory + collecting parts → Rosette kidney

  • Horseshoe kidney → fusion anomaly

  • Persistent fetal lobulation → lobulated kidney

  • Polycystic kidney → cystic developmental disorder

Exam Pearl:
Secretory part + collecting part fail to unite → Rosette kidney.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৫) What is the lining epithelium of DCT?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium. Compared with the PCT, DCT cells are smaller, have fewer mitochondria, and lack a prominent brush border, giving the DCT a relatively clear/wider lumen on histology.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Nephron segment Epithelium
PCT Simple cuboidal + brush border
Loop of Henle (thin segment) Simple squamous
DCT Simple cuboidal, no brush border
Collecting duct Simple cuboidal → columnar

Exam Pearl:
DCT = simple cuboidal epithelium without a brush border.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৬) Which metabolic process occurs in kidney?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The kidney, particularly the renal cortex, is capable of gluconeogenesis, especially during prolonged fasting. It contributes significantly to maintaining blood glucose, alongside the liver. The kidney can synthesize glucose from substrates such as lactate, glycerol, and glutamine.

Although glycolysis, glycogenesis, and glycogenolysis can also occur in renal cells, the classically tested metabolic process associated with the kidney is gluconeogenesis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kidney → gluconeogenesis

  • Major site → renal cortex

  • Especially important during → prolonged fasting

  • Major gluconeogenic substrate → glutamine

  • Liver + kidney → major organs for gluconeogenesis

Exam Pearl:
In fasting, the kidney becomes an important contributor to blood glucose through gluconeogenesis.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৭) What is the site of action of aldosterone?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Aldosterone acts mainly on the late distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, particularly on principal cells. It increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion, helping regulate extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. It also promotes H⁺ secretion indirectly through effects on intercalated cells.

Among the given options, collecting duct (CD) is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aldosterone → late DCT + collecting duct

  • Principal cells → ↑ Na⁺ reabsorption, ↑ K⁺ secretion

  • Intercalated cells → ↑ H⁺ secretion

  • Stimulated by → Angiotensin II and hyperkalemia

Exam Pearl:
Aldosterone acts mainly on the late DCT and collecting duct; in this MCQ, choose Collecting duct.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৮) In an average 70-kilogram man, the combined blood flow through both kidneys is about..... ml/min?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
In an average 70-kg adult, the combined renal blood flow through both kidneys is approximately 1,200 mL/min, which is about 20–25% of the cardiac output.

Renal blood flow is very high because the kidneys continuously receive a large blood supply for glomerular filtration and regulation of body fluid composition.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renal blood flow → ~1200 mL/min

  • Renal plasma flow → ~600–700 mL/min

  • Renal blood flow → about 20–25% of cardiac output

  • GFR → ~125 mL/min

Exam Pearl:
Both kidneys together receive ≈ 1200 mL blood/min.

Renal & body fluids.question: ৯) Components of JG apparatus excludes.....?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The juxtaglomerular (JG) apparatus has three main components:

  1. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells → modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole; secrete renin.

  2. Macula densa cells → specialized cells of the DCT that sense tubular NaCl.

  3. Lacis cells (extraglomerular mesangial cells) → located between the afferent/efferent arterioles and macula densa.

Mesangial cells are associated with the glomerulus and support the capillary tuft, but ordinary/intraglomerular mesangial cells are not considered a component of the JG apparatus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • JG apparatus = JG cells + macula densa + lacis cells

  • JG cells → renin

  • Macula densa → senses NaCl

  • Lacis cells → extraglomerular mesangial cells

  • Mesangial cells → glomerular support/contractile function

Exam Pearl:
JG apparatus = JG cells + macula densa + lacis cells; ordinary mesangial cells are excluded.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১০) What is the value of net filtration pressure(mmHg) in glomeruli?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The net filtration pressure (NFP) across the glomerular capillaries is approximately 10–12 mmHg. In the classic physiology calculation:

  • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure = 60 mmHg

  • Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure = 18 mmHg

  • Plasma colloid osmotic pressure = 28 mmHg

  • Bowman’s capsule colloid osmotic pressure ≈ 0 mmHg

Therefore:

NFP = 60 − (18 + 28) = 14 mmHg

However, many standard physiology texts/exam keys use ~10–12 mmHg as the effective average NFP. Among the given options, 12 mmHg is the best answer.

Exam Pearl:
Glomerular NFP ≈ 10–12 mmHg → choose 12 mmHg.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১১) Which hormone or autacoid increases GFR?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Prostaglandins (especially PGE₂ and PGI₂) cause vasodilation of the renal vasculature, particularly helping maintain renal blood flow and GFR during states of sympathetic activation or vasoconstrictor influence.

In contrast:

  • Epinephrine → renal vasoconstriction → ↓ GFR

  • Norepinephrine → renal vasoconstriction → ↓ GFR

  • Endothelin → potent vasoconstrictor → ↓ renal blood flow and GFR

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Prostaglandins → renal vasodilation → maintain/increase GFR

  • Sympathetic stimulation → ↓ GFR

  • Endothelin → ↓ GFR

  • NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins → may reduce renal perfusion/GFR, especially in susceptible patients.

Exam Pearl:
Renal prostaglandins are protective vasodilators → help maintain GFR.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১২) Which acts as countercurrent exchanger?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
The vasa recta acts as the countercurrent exchanger in the kidney. It consists of specialized straight capillaries that run parallel to the loop of Henle in the medulla. Through passive exchange of water and solutes, the vasa recta helps preserve the medullary osmotic gradient, which is essential for concentrating urine.

The loop of Henle acts as the countercurrent multiplier, while the vasa recta acts as the countercurrent exchanger.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Loop of Henle → countercurrent multiplier

  • Vasa recta → countercurrent exchanger

  • Purpose → maintain medullary osmotic gradient

  • Important for → concentrating urine

Exam Pearl:
Multiplier = Loop of Henle; Exchanger = Vasa recta.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৩) Which is hereditary glomerular disease?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Alport syndrome is a hereditary glomerular disease caused by mutations affecting type IV collagen, an important component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). It classically presents with hematuria, progressive renal impairment, and may be associated with sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities.

  • Nephrotic syndrome (NS) → a clinical syndrome with multiple possible causes.

  • Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) → usually acquired/inflammatory.

  • SLE → autoimmune disease causing secondary glomerular disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Alport syndrome → hereditary nephritis

  • Defect → Type IV collagen

  • Classic triad → hematuria + deafness + ocular abnormalities

  • Inheritance → commonly X-linked

Exam Pearl:
Hereditary glomerular disease = Alport syndrome.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৪) Which is not a feature of nephritic syndrome?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Lipiduria is a characteristic feature of nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic syndrome. Nephritic syndrome is primarily due to glomerular inflammation, leading to:

  • Hematuria — often with RBC casts

  • Oliguria — due to reduced GFR

  • Hypertension — due to sodium and water retention

  • Mild–moderate proteinuria

In contrast, nephrotic syndrome is characterized by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Nephritic Nephrotic
Hematuria Heavy proteinuria
Oliguria Severe edema
Hypertension Hypoalbuminemia
RBC casts Hyperlipidemia + lipiduria
↓ GFR Lipid casts/oval fat bodies

Exam Pearl:
Lipiduria → nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic syndrome.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৫) Lipoid nephrosis is the name of which renal disease?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Lipoid nephrosis is the classical/older name for minimal change disease. It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and is characterized by selective proteinuria, especially albuminuria.

On light microscopy, the glomeruli appear essentially normal. Electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes.

  • Membranous glomerulopathy → diffuse thickening of GBM.

  • IgA nephropathy → mesangial IgA deposition.

  • FSGS → focal and segmental glomerular sclerosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lipoid nephrosis = Minimal change disease

  • Commonest nephrotic syndrome in children

  • LM → normal

  • EM → foot process effacement

  • Usually responds well to corticosteroids

Exam Pearl:
Lipoid nephrosis = Minimal Change Disease (MCD).

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৬) Which is a feature of NS?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Nephrotic syndrome (NS) is characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day in adults), resulting in hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria.

  • Sudden onset → more suggestive of some acute glomerular diseases.

  • History of skin infection → classically associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, a nephritic syndrome.

  • Hypertension → more characteristic of nephritic syndrome; it may occur in NS but is not a defining feature.

  • Massive proteinuria → hallmark of nephrotic syndrome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • NS → massive proteinuria

  • Hypoalbuminemia

  • Edema

  • Hyperlipidemia

  • Lipiduria

Exam Pearl:
Nephrotic syndrome = massive proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + edema.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৭) Lower UTI excludes.....?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Lower urinary tract infections (UTIs) involve structures below the kidneys, including the urethra, urinary bladder, and prostate.

  • Urethritis → infection of urethra → lower UTI

  • Cystitis → infection of bladder → lower UTI

  • Prostatitis → infection/inflammation of prostate → generally classified as lower urinary tract infection in men

  • Pyelitis → inflammation/infection of the renal pelvis → upper UTI

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lower UTI: Urethritis + Cystitis + Prostatitis

  • Upper UTI: Pyelitis + Pyelonephritis

  • Kidney involvement → think upper UTI

Exam Pearl:
Pyelitis = upper UTI; the other three are lower urinary tract infections.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৮) Toxic ATN is most obvious in which part of kidneys?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
In toxic acute tubular necrosis (ATN), tubular injury is most prominent in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) because its cells have a high metabolic demand, abundant mitochondria, and receive high exposure to filtered nephrotoxins.

The PCT is especially vulnerable to toxins such as aminoglycosides, heavy metals, and certain chemical agents. The thick ascending limb can also be affected, particularly in ischemic ATN, but the classic site for toxic injury is the PCT.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Toxic ATN → PCT

  • Ischemic ATN → PCT + thick ascending limb

  • PCT → high metabolic activity → vulnerable to toxins

  • Common nephrotoxins → aminoglycosides, heavy metals

Exam Pearl:
Toxic ATN = PCT is the classic most vulnerable site.

Renal & body fluids.question: ১৯) Which renal tumor is termed as Wilms tumor?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Wilms tumor is the common name for nephroblastoma, a malignant embryonal tumor of the kidney that occurs predominantly in children.

  • Clear cell renal cell carcinoma → common adult renal malignancy.

  • Papillary renal cell carcinoma → another adult renal cell carcinoma subtype.

  • Urothelial carcinoma → arises from the renal pelvis/urothelium.

  • Nephroblastoma → Wilms tumor.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Wilms tumor = Nephroblastoma

  • Common age → children

  • Associated gene → WT1 (11p13)

  • Classic presentation → abdominal mass

Exam Pearl:
Wilms tumor = Nephroblastoma.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২০) Which is not contraindication of renal biopsy?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Isolated hematuria is not a contraindication to renal biopsy. In selected patients with unexplained persistent hematuria, renal biopsy may actually be performed to identify underlying glomerular disease.

The other options are important contraindications or major risk factors:

  • Thrombocytopenia → increased risk of bleeding.

  • Uncontrolled hypertension → increased risk of post-biopsy bleeding.

  • Solitary kidney → traditionally considered a contraindication/relative contraindication because bleeding could threaten the function of the only kidney, although modern practice may permit biopsy in selected cases.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Renal biopsy contraindications → bleeding tendency, uncontrolled hypertension, active infection, etc.

  • Thrombocytopenia → contraindication

  • Uncontrolled HTN → contraindication

  • Solitary kidney → traditionally relative contraindication

  • Isolated hematuria → NOT a contraindication

Exam Pearl:
Among these options, isolated hematuria is the exception.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২১) What is the suggestive cause of myoglobinuria?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Myoglobinuria occurs when skeletal muscle is damaged, releasing myoglobin into the bloodstream, which is then filtered by the kidneys and appears in urine. The classic cause is rhabdomyolysis.

  • Rhabdomyolysis → muscle breakdown → ↑ myoglobin → myoglobinuria

  • Intravascular hemolysis → releases hemoglobin → hemoglobinuria, not myoglobinuria.

  • Infection and tumors are not typical direct causes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Finding Main cause
Myoglobinuria Rhabdomyolysis
Hemoglobinuria Intravascular hemolysis
Both Urine dipstick positive for heme

Exam Pearl:
Myoglobinuria → think rhabdomyolysis.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২২) Which is the most common cause of dysuria?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Cystitis (urinary bladder infection) is the most common cause of dysuria, particularly in women. Dysuria is typically associated with frequency and urgency in acute cystitis.

  • Cystitis → most common cause; often presents with dysuria, frequency, urgency.

  • Urethritis → can cause dysuria, especially with sexually transmitted infections, but is less common overall.

  • Prostatitis → may cause dysuria in men, often with pelvic/perineal pain and urinary symptoms.

  • Pyelitis → usually causes upper urinary tract symptoms and is less likely to present as isolated dysuria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Dysuria → most commonly cystitis

  • Cystitis → dysuria + frequency + urgency

  • Urethritis → consider STI

  • Pyelonephritis → fever + flank pain + dysuria

Exam Pearl:
Most common cause of dysuria = Cystitis.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২৩) Which is the renal cause of AKI?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Interstitial nephritis is an intrinsic (renal) cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) because the primary injury occurs within the kidney, particularly the renal interstitium and tubules.

  • Sepsis → commonly causes pre-renal AKI and/or acute tubular injury, but is not itself a specific intrinsic renal diagnosis.

  • Cardiac failure → pre-renal AKI due to reduced renal perfusion.

  • Interstitial nephritis → intrinsic renal AKI.

  • Urinary calculi → can cause post-renal AKI when obstruction is significant/bilateral.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pre-renal: sepsis, cardiac failure, dehydration

  • Intrinsic renal: ATN, acute interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis

  • Post-renal: stones, tumors, prostate enlargement

Exam Pearl:
AKI → Pre-renal / Intrinsic renal / Post-renal; interstitial nephritis is an intrinsic renal cause.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২৪) Which is true about CRF?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Chronic renal failure (CRF), now generally termed chronic kidney disease (CKD), is characterized by progressive and usually irreversible loss of renal function.

  • Irreversible → True; established CKD generally cannot be completely reversed.

  • Normal-sized kidneys → usually kidneys become small and contracted in advanced CKD, although exceptions include diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis, and some infiltrative diseases.

  • Hypotension → not a typical defining feature; hypertension is common.

  • No anemia → false; normocytic normochromic anemia is a common complication due to reduced erythropoietin production.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CKD → progressive, usually irreversible

  • Advanced CKD → small kidneys (with exceptions)

  • Common complication → normocytic normochromic anemia

  • Hypertension → common

  • ↓ Erythropoietin → anemia

Exam Pearl:
CRF/CKD = progressive irreversible renal dysfunction + anemia + commonly hypertension.

Renal & body fluids.question: ২৫) What is the cause of CRF without anemia?
Renal & body fluids.exp:
Polycystic kidney disease (PCKD/ADPKD) is a classic cause of chronic renal failure with relatively preserved hemoglobin, because the enlarged cystic kidneys may continue to produce erythropoietin (EPO). Therefore, the anemia commonly expected in advanced CKD may be less severe or absent.

  • DM → CKD commonly causes significant anemia.

  • Hydronephrosis → can cause CKD, but anemia is not a classic distinguishing feature.

  • Amyloidosis → CKD with anemia may occur.

  • PCKD → classical exception: CRF may occur without marked anemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CKD → anemia usually due to ↓ EPO

  • PCKD → anemia may be absent/less severe

  • PCKD → bilaterally enlarged kidneys

  • Other classic CKD exception with large kidneys → diabetic nephropathy

Exam Pearl:
CRF without anemia → think PCKD (especially ADPKD).
